section_1.title: The Putnam Mindset: Beyond Calculation
section_1.content: Transition from mechanical computation to 'Pattern Recognition'. Introduce the core philosophy: Putnam problems prioritize elegant, often non-obvious insights over brute-force algebra.
section_1.example: A squirrel hiding nuts in a grid: Instead of calculating every spot, use the Pigeonhole Principle to prove at least one cache contains a specific density.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Toolkit: The Power of Invariants
section_2.content: Define 'Invariants'—properties that remain unchanged despite dynamic transformations. Use a visual graph showing a system evolving while a central 'knot' remains constant.
section_2.example: A robot changing colors on a chessboard: If a move always flips adjacent squares, the parity of the colors remains invariant. We use this to solve complex tiling problems.

section_3.title: Strategic Heuristics: Extreme Principle & Descent
section_3.content: Introduce the 'Extreme Principle': If a set exists, consider the most extreme element (max/min). Visual: A mountain peak diagram where identifying the summit collapses the search space.
section_3.example: Consider a set of points in the plane; look at the pair with the minimum distance. This 'local' extreme often forces a 'global' constraint that solves the problem instantly.

section_4.title: Symmetry and Reduction
section_4.content: Teach how to reduce complexity by identifying symmetries. Use visual overlays of rotational or reflective symmetry applied to complex geometric equations to simplify them.
section_4.example: A spinning mechanical gear system: By assuming rotational symmetry, we can reduce a 10-variable system into a single representative variable equation.

section_5.title: Putting it Together: The Final Proof Architecture
section_5.content: Summarize the 'Look, Simplify, Solve' workflow. Emphasize that a clear logical narrative (the proof) is as important as the numerical result.
section_5.example: Final walkthrough: A complex integral problem solved by recognizing a hidden symmetry (a secret mirror image in the function) that makes the area cancel out to zero.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
